name: Dentist deep cleaning (scaling and root planing)

lead: Scaling and root planing, usually called deep cleaning, removes plaque and hardened deposits from below the gumline and smooths the root surfaces. The payoff people want is calmer, less swollen gums, less gum-related breath odour and teeth that stay in place and frame the smile.

Ultrasonic scalers and hand instruments clear bacterial deposits from root surfaces and pockets so inflamed gums can settle and reattach more easily. It is the standard first-line treatment for periodontitis, the disease behind receding gums and tooth loss, and guidelines recommend it as initial therapy.

paras: A dentist or hygienist does it in the chair, usually under local anaesthetic, often one section of the mouth per visit. It is followed by regular maintenance visits and consistent home care, which is what keeps the results in place.

Reported effects include post-procedure discomfort, tooth sensitivity, possible damage to cracked enamel or restorations, and aerosol generation. Pockets deeper than about 6 mm may need surgery. Results depend on home care and maintenance visits.

chain: Plaque and calculus removed below gumline
Healthier, firmer gums and fresher breath
angle.text: Deep cleaning removes the plaque and deposits below the gumline that keep gums inflamed, so gums look calmer and less swollen, breath improves and the teeth framing the smile are protected. The cosmetic gains come from treating the gum disease itself.

lead: Scaling and root planing, often called deep cleaning, is a non-surgical dental procedure that removes plaque and calculus from tooth surfaces above and below the gumline and smooths the exposed root surfaces. It is the usual first step in treating periodontitis, the gum disease that causes gum pockets, bone loss and eventual tooth loss [1][2].

For appearance, it matters because inflamed, bleeding or swollen gums and receding gum lines change how a smile looks, and because treating periodontitis aims to keep teeth in place and gums firm so that the smile, tooth spacing and facial support are preserved. People use it to calm gum inflammation, reduce puffy or bleeding gums, and remove the calculus build-up that stains and roughens teeth. Guidelines cited in encyclopedic sources recommend it as initial therapy, and a 2002 review called it the 'gold standard' against which newer periodontal treatments are compared [1][3].

Periodontitis is common: a 2021 review reports that it affects more than 40 percent of adults in the United States, and that the severe form has a global prevalence of 11 percent [4]. Research on scaling and root planing covers clinical trials of instrumentation and adjuncts, and studies of how periodontal treatment relates to conditions such as diabetes [5][6]. Public-health and clinical sources describe how it fits into a wider routine of home care, professional maintenance and, where needed, gum surgery [7][8].

paras: Wikipedia's article on periodontal disease lists gum recession, bleeding gums, loose teeth and bad breath among the signs, and notes that gum inflammation and bone loss are usually painless, so the condition can advance before treatment is sought [8]. Gingivitis, the early stage, makes gums swollen, red and prone to bleeding; periodontitis is the stage in which gums pull away from the teeth, bone is lost and teeth may loosen or fall out [8]. Deep cleaning targets the bacterial deposits driving that inflammation, so that gums settle and the supporting bone is preserved [2][8]. Smoking is described as the most important environmental risk factor, with diabetes and family history among others [8].

The US National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research lists swollen, red, tender or bleeding gums, receding gums that make teeth look longer, loose teeth and persistent bad breath among the signs of periodontal disease [7]. Receding gums and loss of supporting bone are the changes most visible in a smile, and bone loss is described as permanent [1][8].

The treated area is usually numbed and typically one quadrant or half of the mouth is treated per visit. Ultrasonic scalers and hand instruments such as curettes remove deposits and smooth the roots. Optional additions include chlorhexidine rinses, locally placed antibiotics and lasers [1]. A whole-mouth approach completed in about 24 hours was proposed by a Leuven group in 1995 [1].

Scaling removes plaque and calculus from the crown and root surfaces; root planing smooths the root and may remove some cementum or dentine contaminated by toxins or microbes [1]. A regular cleaning (scaling and polishing) does not include root planing, and polishing removes some plaque and stain but not calculus [1].

Tools include ultrasonic (magnetostrictive or piezoelectric) and sonic scalers, plus hand instruments such as scalers and curettes. Ultrasonic units also deliver lavage fluid, which can carry antimicrobials. Ultrasonic scalers may be faster and need less force than hand instruments, which may lower repetitive-stress risk for hygienists, though studies disagree on whether they are more effective, and hand instruments often finish the job [1].

Patients are usually numbed in the treated area, and only one half or one quarter of the mouth is treated per visit, because numbing the whole mouth causes difficulty eating or drinking and risk of self-biting [1]. Traditional debridement uses four sessions two weeks apart; a Leuven group proposed full-mouth treatment within about 24 hours in 1995 [1]. In one comparison, full-mouth ultrasonic debridement averaged 3.3 minutes per pocket versus 8.8 minutes per pocket for quadrant scaling and root planing, with no statistically significant difference in improvement [1].

Bacterial contamination of root surfaces is shallow, so extensive removal of cementum is not considered necessary for healing, and some full-mouth protocols aim to disrupt biofilm in the pocket without removing cementum [1].

Scaling refers to removing plaque and calculus from the crown and the root surface; root planing smooths the root so that bacteria adhere less easily. A 2021 commentary emphasises that subgingival calculus is covered with a biofilm of metabolically active bacteria, that periodontal inflammation is related to calculus and biofilm, and that the primary goal is to remove these deposits [2]. A 2021 review notes that initial non-surgical therapy consists primarily of home-care review and scaling and root planing, and that residual sites with active disease can then be considered for further treatment [4].

Scaling and root planing is indicated for periodontitis, for pockets deeper than about 4 mm where brushing and flossing cannot reach, and as initial therapy in severe periodontitis before any surgery [1]. A dentist or hygienist measures pockets with a small probe; healthy pockets are usually 1 to 3 mm, and X-rays can show bone loss [7]. Wikipedia reports that pockets deeper than 3 mm generally cannot be cleaned adequately at home, and that at 6 to 7 mm professional instruments may not reach all plaque [8]. The 2017 classification divides periodontitis into four stages and three grades, with smoking and diabetes able to raise a patient's grade [8].

Chlorhexidine irrigation has high substantivity, is prescription-only in the US and is not intended for long-term use; povidone-iodine is an alternative where there is no contraindication [1]. Site-specific antibiotics such as minocycline microspheres are placed in pockets and release slowly [1]. Lasers may be used after scaling and root planing to promote healing [1]. Low-dose doxycycline may be given alongside scaling, and evidence for systemic antibiotics is described as low-certainty [8]. Trials have tested local and systemic metronidazole [9] and Lactobacillus reuteri lozenges as adjuncts [10]. Surgery such as flap surgery, bone grafts or guided tissue regeneration by a periodontist is used for severe or non-responding cases [1][8].

A 2002 review of the clinical evidence reports that analysis of Egyptian hieroglyphics and medical papyri indicates non-surgical periodontal treatment was common 3000 to 4000 years ago [3]. It describes a consistency of response across manual, sonic and ultrasonic instrumentation, and a newer paradigm of complete-mouth disinfection [3].

Wikipedia's periodontal disease article notes that gum disease has been found in an ancient hominid about 3 million years old and in the Iceman Ötzi, and that archaeological plaque DNA suggests it became more common as cereals entered the diet [8].

A 2018 Cochrane review found routine scale and polish made little to no difference for adults without severe periodontitis, but did not study root planing. A 2016 review found root planing was linked to reduced plaque and improved gingival index scores at three and six months [1]. Effectiveness is reported to decline when pockets exceed 6 mm, which may then need surgery, and home care and maintenance attendance strongly influence long-term results [1].

Wikipedia reports that scaling and root planing usually succeeds where pockets are 4 to 5 mm or shallower, and that mild to moderate periodontitis responds well to thorough treatment [8][1]. The 2002 review reports consistent clinical responses across manual, sonic and ultrasonic instruments in chronic periodontitis [3]. A 2021 review notes that after initial therapy, residual sites with active disease can be considered for further treatment [4].

A randomized multi-centre study in general practice assigned 95 dental hygienists in 59 clinics to one of two non-surgical protocols: establishing self-performed oral hygiene before a single session of ultrasonic instrumentation, or conventional non-surgical therapy with patient education [11]. A placebo-controlled trial of 30 chronic periodontitis patients tested Lactobacillus reuteri lozenges as an adjunct to full-mouth scaling and root planing, with follow-up at 3, 6, 9 and 12 weeks [10].

Soft tissue begins healing once biofilm and calculus are removed, while gains in gum attachment are slow and lost bone does not return [1]. A re-evaluation is usually done four to six weeks later, with re-measurement at about 90 days; pockets that remain deep and bleed on probing suggest continuing disease and may lead to surgery or adjunctive therapy [8][1]. Plaque tends to return to pre-cleaning levels in about three to four months, so maintenance cleanings every three to four months and daily home care are typical [8][1]. Surgically treated patients on maintenance care halted tooth loss in nearly 85 percent of cases in long-term studies cited by Wikipedia [8].

Daily home care described in the sources includes brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, flossing or interdental brushes, and quitting tobacco, which slows healing and can make treatment less effective [1][7]. Adjunct and surgical comparisons continue, including a 2024 split-mouth trial of scaling and root planing during minimally invasive surgery [12] and five-year radiological findings from a trial of four treatment strategies [13].

Smoking is described as the most important environmental risk factor; diabetes roughly doubles to triples risk; other factors include family history, hormonal changes, stress and certain medications [8][7]. Wikipedia describes much of the tissue damage as arising from the host's immune response to bacteria such as Porphyromonas gingivalis [8].

Studies have examined periodontal treatment alongside systemic conditions. A Cochrane review evaluated periodontal treatment for glycaemic control in people with diabetes [5], and a meta-analysis of randomized trials examined the effect of scaling and root planing on glycated haemoglobin and C-reactive protein in type 2 diabetes [14].

Wikipedia notes periodontitis is associated with higher inflammatory markers and with cardiovascular disease, and that these links are associations rather than proven causes; a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence that periodontal treatment lowers blood pressure [8]. A completed registered trial, the Kidney and Periodontal Disease Study, enrolled 51 people with chronic kidney disease and periodontal disease [15].

Discomfort is expected afterwards, and root surfaces can be damaged, which may cause tooth or root sensitivity. Ultrasonic scaling can damage cracked enamel, early decay and resin restorations, and generates aerosols that can spread pathogens [1]. Peak bacteremia occurs within 5 minutes of the procedure [6]. A 2023 review discusses scaling and root planing in a patient with atherosclerosis, arrhythmia and anticoagulation [16].

The 2015 Global Burden of Disease estimated 538 million people affected by periodontal disease, and chronic periodontitis affected about 10.8 percent of the world population in 2010; lost productivity from severe periodontitis is estimated at about US$54 billion a year [8]. In the United States, 30 to 50 percent of people are affected to some degree, about 10 percent severely [8].

Trials of scaling and root planing include a randomized multi-centre study in general practice that assigned 95 dental hygienists in 59 clinics to one of two non-surgical protocols [11], a placebo-controlled trial of Lactobacillus reuteri lozenges as an adjunct in 30 patients [10], and trials of local and systemic metronidazole [9]. A Cochrane review and a meta-analysis of randomized trials examined diabetes outcomes [5][14].

A 2024 split-mouth randomized trial examined scaling and root planing during minimally invasive surgery [12], and five-year radiographic findings from a trial of four periodontitis treatment strategies appeared in 2023 [13]. Other registered studies concern gum tissue classification, dental anxiety in children and crown lengthening, and do not test deep cleaning itself [17][18][19][20]. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of bacteremia after dental procedures found peak bacteremia within 5 minutes, with extractions showing the highest incidence (62 to 66 percent) and scaling and root planing lower but substantial [6].
